case_study_insert.main_stem: Pinecrest Health Centre (PHC) is a partnership in the healthcare sector, employing a workforce of 60. Founded in 2008 by Dr Sofia Pinecrest, it provides private outpatient consultations and diagnostic scans and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. PHC plans to invest $680,000 in a new minor-operations suite and scanner, financed by a $400,000 ten-year bank loan and $280,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $300,000 a year, a variable cost of $8.00 a unit and a selling price of $14.00, and currently produces 90,000 units a year, each a patient visit. Demand from local employers has grown steadily. PHC faces two problems: patient waiting times have risen and nursing absenteeism has reached 10%.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Quality Report, Q4 2025: The diagnostics pilot handled 21,000 patient visits last quarter with a re-scan rate of 2.7%, down from 4.4% a year ago. Patient complaints about appointment delays fell from 61 to 28 per month. Average waiting time is 38 minutes. A survey of 700 patients found 66% would pay up to $0.80 more for same-day scans and 59% check waiting-time ratings before choosing a clinic. Records show 22 of 60 staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new scanner; external accreditation courses cost $950 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Pinecrest Health Centre for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.0% to 4.75%, increasing the cost of variable-rate borrowing. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 7.2% from $13.10 to $14.04 per hour, pushing up wage costs in healthcare. (3) Medical consumables and energy input costs have risen 10.5% year-on-year, private-healthcare inflation is 6.8%, and consumer spending on private clinics grew 4.1% over the same period.

questions.question_text: PHC plans to fund part of its $680,000 minor-operations suite with a $400,000 ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for PHC of using retained profit rather than the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit brings no interest bill or fixed repayment schedule, so the $280,000 drawn from past profits protects the partnership's cash flow while it meets fixed costs of $300,000 a year. Cash saved can absorb the 10.5% rise in medical consumables and energy costs without raising the $14.00 price, preserving the $6.00 contribution on 90,000 patient visits.

Point 2: Retained profit avoids the collateral and default risk of the $400,000 loan, so the new scanner suite cannot be threatened if patient numbers disappoint. It also keeps decision-making with Dr Sofia Pinecrest and the partners, since no lender can impose conditions. Because it is already in the business, it can be released at once to cut the 38-minute waiting time and address the 10% nursing absenteeism. Its hierarchical structure can then direct the cash saved specifically to cutting the 38-minute waiting time that patients complain about while the new scanner suite beds in.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of retained profit over a bank loan (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to PHC, its suite, costs and services.

questions.question_text: PHC is promoting its new minor-operations suite. Consider advertising in local newspapers, sponsoring a regional healthcare conference, or targeted social media and email marketing to existing patients. Which should PHC choose? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Local newspaper advertising: Newspaper adverts would reach the local community and build awareness of the new suite. Costs are moderate but readership is ageing and falling, and a general audience includes many who will never need private scans, so much of the spend is wasted for a 60-staff partnership committing $680,000. The message is also static and hard to measure.

Regional healthcare conference sponsorship: This would put PHC in front of GPs and employers who refer patients, and allows demonstration of the scanner, supporting the 59% of surveyed patients who check waiting-time ratings. It is prestigious but a costly one-off event with limited reach; with 700 patients surveyed and 21,000 visits last quarter, one conference alone cannot fill 90,000 visits a year.

Targeted social media and email marketing: Digital messages to existing patients can promote same-day scans directly to the 66% who would pay $0.80 more, show current waiting times and be tracked cheaply. Content can be updated as the 38-minute waiting time falls. The weakness is that some patients ignore email and word-of-mouth still drives clinic choice, so personal reminders from reception staff would help.

Recommendation: PHC should choose targeted social media and email marketing, supported by a small conference presence. It reaches the 66% willing to pay $0.80 more at low cost and can run continuously to sustain 90,000 visits, unlike a single event. Newspapers are rejected as wasteful and declining; major conference sponsorship is rejected as too expensive and one-off for a partnership already servicing a $400,000 loan.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies promotional options with limited reference to PHC's survey or services.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discusses advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of PHC with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three options with a justified recommendation that explains why newspapers and conference sponsorship are rejected.

questions.question_text: PHC's nursing absenteeism has reached 10% and waiting times have risen. Explain two benefits for PHC of introducing a performance-related bonus for its nursing staff.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A performance-related bonus links part of pay to measurable targets such as reducing the 38-minute waiting time and keeping the 2.7% re-scan rate low, giving the 60 staff a clear financial incentive (Herzberg's motivator) to improve service quality. Faster appointments would strengthen the appeal of same-day scans to the 66% of surveyed patients willing to pay $0.80 more.

Point 2: Bonuses can lift morale and reduce the 10% nursing absenteeism, because staff see a direct reward for consistent attendance and accuracy. That keeps more of the 22 of 60 staff currently without scanner training at work to use the $680,000 suite, protecting the $6.00 contribution per visit and helping PHC recover the $950 per employee accreditation cost through better performance. Linking part of pay to punctuality also gives supervisors an objective appraisal measure within the hierarchical structure, satisfying the 59% of patients who check waiting-time ratings and giving fair evidence for bonus payments.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit of a performance-related bonus (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to PHC's absenteeism, waiting time and scan quality.

questions.question_text: PHC must train 22 of its 60 staff on the new scanner. Consider on-the-job training or external accreditation courses costing $950 per employee. Which should PHC choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Training beside the scanner suits PHC's own equipment and procedures, costs no course fees and keeps the 22 staff seeing patients while they learn. That protects the 21,000 visits handled last quarter and the drop in re-scan rate from 4.4% to 2.7%. The drawbacks are that trainer-staff see fewer patients themselves, local habits can be passed on, and there is no external qualification, which may matter for a private clinic keen on professional credibility.

External accreditation courses: At $950 per employee, accreditation for all 22 costs $20,900 ($950 x 22), affordable against the $680,000 investment, and gives recognised skills that reassure patients. However, it removes 22 of 60 staff from the clinic temporarily, worsening the 38-minute waiting time and 10% absenteeism, and generic content may not match PHC's scanner, so follow-up coaching would still be needed. The $20,900 also competes with the 10% absenteeism problem, since releasing 22 of 60 staff for paid training is a major commitment for a partnership with revenue of $3,600,000.

Decision: PHC should choose on-the-job training initially, with accreditation for senior radiographers later. It is cheaper, equipment-specific and avoids lengthening waiting lists while absenteeism is 10%; full external training is rejected because the $20,900 and the loss of 22 staff would disrupt the 90,000-visit target and patient satisfaction, and accreditation can be added once the scanner is running smoothly, beginning with senior radiographers who demonstrate it to patients; the rest can follow once the suite is profitable, keeping the 90,000-visit plan on track.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Describes the two training methods with little application to PHC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the benefits and drawbacks of each method in the context of PHC's costs, capacity and staffing.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods with a justified decision that rejects the alternative and refers to cost, waiting-time disruption and equipment relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how PHC's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $300,000 ÷ ($14.00 − $8.00) = $300,000 ÷ $6.00 = 50,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 50,000 patient visits a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $14.00 − $8.00 = $6.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $6.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways PHC's management can use this cost and break-even data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 50,000-visit break-even output with 90,000 actual visits to find a margin of safety of 40,000 visits (90,000 − 50,000), showing the $680,000 suite can absorb a fall in demand.
2. Use the $6.00 contribution to test the survey: at 90,000 visits a $0.80 premium could add $72,000 (90,000 x $0.80), funding the $950 accreditation courses.
3. Check that contribution covers fixed costs of $300,000 and interest on the $400,000 loan before expanding the suite, so finance costs do not raise break-even.
4. Benchmark average total cost of about $11.33 ($300,000 ÷ 90,000 + $8.00) each quarter to detect waste from the 2.7% re-scan rate and judge whether 10.5% input-cost inflation is being absorbed.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 50,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $6.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses: a margin of safety of 40,000 visits against 90,000 output; a $0.80 premium adding $72,000; covering $300,000 fixed costs and $400,000 loan interest; and unit-cost benchmarking at about $11.33 to track 10.5% input inflation.

working_marks: 1 mark for the correct formula and accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate PHC's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has PHC's financial performance improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 40.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 43.5%
Profit Margin 2024 = 16.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 17.0%
ROCE 2024 = 20.0%
ROCE 2025 = 21.9%

Detailed workings: Gross profit of $1,200,000 on revenue of $3,000,000 in 2024 gives 1,200 ÷ 3,000 = 40.0%; in 2025 gross profit of $1,566,000 on $3,600,000 gives 1,566 ÷ 3,600 = 43.5%. Operating profit of $480,000 ÷ $3,000,000 = 16.0% in 2024 and $612,000 ÷ $3,600,000 = 17.0% in 2025. The return on capital employed divides operating profit by capital employed: $480,000 ÷ $2,400,000 = 20.0% and $612,000 ÷ $2,800,000 = 21.9%. Cost of sales of $1,800,000 and $2,034,000 reconciles exactly with gross profit in both years.

Evaluation: Each measure improved. The rise from 40.0% to 43.5% shows more revenue retained after direct costs, as revenue grew $600,000 while cost of sales rose only $234,000, so most of the additional revenue became gross profit. Operating profitability improved from 16.0% to 17.0%, indicating overheads were held down as patient visits grew. The return on capital increased from 20.0% to 21.9%, so the $2,800,000 of capital employed is working harder, which supports the $680,000 suite. Interest payable fell from $60,000 to $52,000, easing the burden on the partnership.

Conclusion: PHC's financial performance has improved. All three margins rose, the return on capital strengthened and interest payable fell, leaving the partnership better able to service the $400,000 loan. Management must still reduce the 38-minute waiting time and 10% nursing absenteeism, which could erode these gains.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the three measures for both years with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of revenue, cost of sales, capital employed and interest movements and a justified conclusion on whether performance improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for PHC of offering same-day diagnostic scans.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Same-day scans match the survey evidence that 66% of patients would pay up to $0.80 more and 59% check waiting-time ratings. At 90,000 visits an $0.80 premium could add $72,000 (90,000 x $0.80), protecting the $6.00 contribution per visit against 10.5% input-cost inflation and strengthening the case for the $680,000 suite. Faster access would differentiate PHC from local rivals and could lift the 21,000 visits handled last quarter toward the 90,000-unit target and use the new scanner more fully.

Disadvantage: Offering same-day capacity raises the $8.00 variable cost per scan through extra consumables and staff cover, squeezing margins unless the $0.80 premium is widely accepted. It may also worsen the 38-minute waiting time and the 10% nursing absenteeism if staff are stretched, while any rise in the 2.7% re-scan rate would damage the reputation that attracts privately paying patients. As the insert gives no extra-cost figure for same-day capacity, this pressure is stated qualitatively.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to PHC's survey data, costs and services.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 4.75%, the 7.2% minimum wage increase and the 10.5% rise in input costs will affect PHC. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.0% to 4.75%): If PHC's $400,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, the 0.75 percentage-point increase adds 0.75% x $400,000 = $3,000 a year (0.0075 x $400,000), modest against fixed costs of $300,000, and zero if the loan is fixed-rate. Higher rates may also make privately insured patients more cautious about spending. PHC can reduce this risk by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage increase (7.2%, to $14.04 an hour): With a workforce of 60 and 90,000 visits, labour productivity is 90,000 ÷ 60 = 1,500 visits per worker. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay, so an annual wage bill cannot be invented; the defensible check is whether each worker maintains about 1,500 visits. With absenteeism at 10%, a productivity fall would raise unit labour costs and shrink the $6.00 contribution.

Input-cost inflation (10.5% in consumables and energy): The insert gives a variable cost of $8.00 per visit but does not decompose it, so only an illustrative bound is honest. If the whole $8.00 rose 10.5%, that is 10.5% x $8.00 = $0.84 per visit; across 90,000 visits that is about $75,600 a year (90,000 x $0.84). Even a smaller $0.60 rise would cost $54,000 a year (90,000 x $0.60), pulling contribution from $6.00 toward $5.40.

Conclusion: The 10.5% rise in input costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to all 90,000 visits and directly erodes the $6.00 contribution supporting the $680,000 suite, and at up to about $75,600 a year it is far larger than the conditional $3,000 interest cost. The wage rise is significant but cannot be quantified from the insert and depends on 1,500-visit productivity holding, while interest risk is small and fixable. PHC should renegotiate suppliers and recover part of the cost through the $0.80 same-day premium.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to PHC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on PHC's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes with a justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller, with arithmetic shown from insert figures.
